Damage-Size Sensitivity in AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Multi-model performance, ranking stability, and diffusion uncertainty across nested missing-region sizes

Notebook: 23 — Damage-Size Sensitivity Analysis
Design: five matched painting trajectories, seven requested damage levels from 2% to 20%
Quality comparison: OpenCV Telea, LaMa, and Stable Diffusion Inpainting
Uncertainty comparison: four Stable Diffusion seeds per case from Notebook 22
Independent unit: painting trajectory
Status: completed analysis with validated canonical inputs

Executive conclusions

  • OpenCV Telea had the lowest adverse slope on 7 of 11 quality anchors.
  • The top-ranked model across the seven levels came from 1 distinct model(s). Low-damage levels most often favoured LaMa; levels from 10% upward most often favoured LaMa.
  • 5 of 5 main Stable Diffusion uncertainty components increased with damage size.
  • The smallest attainable observed exact-test p-value was 0.0625. With five independent paintings, absence of q ≤ 0.05 evidence must not be read as proof of no effect.
Central conclusion. Damage size changes measured restoration behaviour, but the result depends on model, metric, and painting. The evidence does not support one unconditional winner or one universal damage threshold.
35 cases Seven nested levels across five paintings
11 anchors Kept separate rather than merged into one score
1 winner(s) Across seven family-balanced rankings
5/5 Main uncertainty slopes above zero
0.0001 pp Largest target-versus-realized area error

1. What was evaluated?

The experiment measures how restoration evidence changes when the same five paintings receive increasingly large nested missing regions. The 35 cases are repeated observations from five paintings, not 35 independent artworks.

Evaluation scope

Evidence population Count Interpretation
Controlled damage-size cases 35 Seven nested damage levels for each of five paintings
Restoration candidates 105 OpenCV Telea, LaMa, and Stable Diffusion
Quality anchors 11 Separate reference, perceptual, feature, spatial, texture, colour, seam, and semantic evidence
Independent trajectories 5 Paintings—not the 35 repeated cases—are independent

Declared painting coverage

Painting

p043
  • RQ1: quality is represented by separate metric families.
  • RQ2: methods are compared through matched slopes, paired contrasts, rankings, and restoration evidence.
  • RQ3: repeated-seed variability is reported as empirical uncertainty, not calibrated confidence.
One painting represents each declared category, and three paintings lack classified style metadata. Category and style effects are therefore not estimated.
Section conclusion. The design supports matched damage-size comparisons for these five paintings. It does not support population-wide category or style claims.

2. Were the damage levels constructed correctly?

Controlled-damage integrity checks

Integrity check Observed Conclusion
Area within configured tolerance 35/35 cases Requested and realized damaged areas remained aligned.
Nested with previous damage level 35/35 cases The controlled progression retained its nested design.
Component count preserved 35/35 cases Component behaviour remained traceable across levels.
Touches content boundary 0/35 cases Boundary contact is disclosed rather than ignored.
Largest area error 0.0001 percentage points Area-generation error was small relative to the 2%–20% experimental range.
Section conclusion. All controlled cases remained close to their requested damaged area; the largest absolute error was 0.0001 percentage points. The nested progression is sufficiently controlled for the within-painting sensitivity analysis.
Controlled digital masks do not reproduce the physical, chemical, and historical complexity of naturally aged damage.

4. What did the restorations look like as damage increased?

The image panels place masks, damaged inputs, and matched model outputs side by side. They make edge continuity, smoothing, colour drift, texture loss, and unsupported generated content visible.

Section conclusion. Larger regions expose different weaknesses in different visual contexts. Structured edges, textured brushwork, and portrait or figure content should therefore be interpreted separately rather than reduced to one visual-quality statement.
These panels explain metric behaviour but are not historical authenticity assessments and are not a conservation approval.

12. What does the evidence support?

Supported by this experiment

  • Damage size changes measured restoration behaviour.
  • OpenCV Telea had the lowest adverse slope on 7 of 11 anchors.
  • Family-balanced rankings can be checked against leave-one-painting-out stability.
  • Stable Diffusion seed variability can change with damage size, and its spatial location can be inspected.
  • Metric disagreement and painting-specific differences are meaningful evidence that should remain visible.

Not supported by this experiment

  • One universal damage threshold for restoration failure.
  • One unconditional best model for every painting and metric.
  • Category effects separated from painting identity.
  • Style or historical-period effects.
  • A general deterministic-versus-generative class effect.
  • Historical authenticity or conservation approval.
  • The claim that low uncertainty proves correctness.
Section conclusion. The strongest defensible result is conditional: damage size matters, but interpretation must retain model, metric, painting, visual context, and uncertainty provenance.

13. Final contribution to the thesis

This experiment adds damage extent as an explicit axis in the trustworthy evaluation framework. It connects restoration quality, model ranking, visual failure modes, runtime, morphology, and Stable Diffusion variability without collapsing them into one unsupported index.

  • For RQ1: quality must remain multi-dimensional.
  • For RQ2: model comparisons must be conditional on damage size and painting context.
  • For RQ3: uncertainty is useful as transparent variability evidence, but not as confidence or truth.
Final conclusion. Trustworthy AI-assisted painting restoration requires separate evidence families, matched comparisons, visible failure cases, explicit uncertainty limits, and conservator judgement outside the computational ranking.
The conclusions apply to the evaluated paintings, masks, models, prompts, seeds, and metric implementations. They do not establish historical authenticity and are not a conservation approval.
